_comment: Randomisation ranges for step 4. Every entry carries `evidence`, and the
only three values it may take are:
measured  a number this repository actually produced — a CAD mass, a ROM
spec      a vendor number. Real, but it describes the datasheet servo, not
guessed   nobody has measured this. The range is wide ON PURPOSE: a policy
that survives a wide guess survives the measurement, and a policy
trained on a narrow guess is trained on a fiction.
Ranges are multiplicative on the nominal unless the key ends in _abs, which
means the range is the value itself in SI. Sampled once per environment at
reset, held for the episode: these are manufacturing and assembly spreads,
not noise, and a policy that sees them resampled every step learns to average
them away instead of being robust to them.
params/st3215.json is NOT a fit (actuator.load() says so out loud). Until
robot/bench/fit_bam.py has run, the actuator entries below are the width of
our ignorance about the servo, and they are deliberately wider than a fit
would justify. Narrow them when there is a fit, and not before.

k_u.why: torque per volt. eta = k_u*R/k_e = 0.43 from the three vendor numbers, which is low even for a 1:345 spur stack — either the gearbox really is that lossy or a spec is optimistic. Both mean the true value is somewhere inside a band this wide.

k_e.why: back-EMF, hence the no-load speed. Pinned by 4.71 rad/s @ 12 V, which is the vendor number most likely to be honest — it is measured with no load, where there is nothing to be optimistic about.

R.why: 4.44 ohm from the 2.7 A locked-rotor spec, at the terminals. Wiring, connector and the bus daisy-chain add series resistance the spec does not include, so the spread is asymmetric upward.

J_m.why: reflected rotor inertia, and check_model.py reports it dominates the leg at ~73x the knee link's own. The single most consequential guess in the model: it sets how fast the joint can change direction at all.

tau_c.why: Coulomb friction. Varies servo to servo with grease and preload more than any other term, and it is what makes a leg stick near a reversal.

b_v.why: viscous friction. Not separable from the back-EMF damping k_w without current measurement at several supply voltages (actuator.py, 'Identifiability'), so it is guessed wide and will stay guessed until the bench runs both.

kp.why: the servo's own inner-loop gain after register scaling. We do not own this loop and have never read the registers back off a real unit.

deadband_abs.why: registers 26/27, in encoder steps of 0.088 deg. 0 to 4 steps. Zero is a servo configured tight; 4 steps is the factory default region and is what makes a bus servo buzz around its target.

punch_abs.why: register 24, the minimum drive applied once outside the dead zone. Never read off a real servo.

u_bat_abs.why: a 3S LiPo from 3.3 to 4.2 V per cell. This is the whole reason actuator.py is a voltage law: stall torque and no-load speed fall TOGETHER as the pack drains, and a policy that only ever saw 12 V has never met the robot it will run on at the end of a session.

sag_ohm_abs.why: series resistance of pack, harness and the bus daisy-chain, in ohms. The load case is all twelve pulling together, and the model applies it to the SUMMED current, so the number is smaller than it looks: twelve servos at 3.6 A each into 0.06 ohm is a 2.6 V sag, which is already at the top of what a healthy 3S pack does. The first range here was 0.18, which is 7.8 V and not a battery. Nobody has put a scope on it.

delay_s_abs.why: command latency from the policy writing a target to the servo acting on it, quantised to the 20 ms control tick. params/bus_timing.json does not exist yet — robot/bench/bus_probe.py writes it — so this is one whole control period of ignorance, which is the honest width. robot/README.md 'The 50 Hz budget' shows the FTDI latency timer alone ships at 16 ms.

mass_scale.why: link masses are real solids in 3d/mini_dog.py, so this is print-density and hardware spread, not ignorance. Tight on purpose — widening a measured number to be safe throws away the measurement.

com_offset_m_abs.why: where the battery, the Pi and the harness actually end up. The CAD knows the structure's centre of mass; it does not know how the wiring was dressed.

payload_kg_abs.why: a mass added at the payload bay, up to 12 % of the robot. What the bay is for.

friction.why: tangential friction of a printed foot on whatever it is standing on. check_model.py names it a guess and says a tilt test measures it in an afternoon; until then the range spans lino to carpet.

box_height_m_abs.why: procedural boxes scattered under the robot, in metres. The top of the range is a quarter of the shin, which is roughly where a trot stops coping and a policy has to.

box_density.why: fraction of the tiles under the robot that are raised at all. Zero is flat ground, and every environment gets it some of the time on purpose.

interval_s_abs.why: seconds between shoves. Not a model of anything — a way to keep the policy from learning a gait that only survives from a standing start.

vel_m_s_abs.why: instantaneous velocity added to the base, m/s, in a random horizontal direction.
